# Repository overview
This system is Flask, a web framework whose Application Core orchestrates application construction, routing, request dispatch, response handling, contexts, configuration, sessions, templates, errors, and WSGI execution. CLI And Testing adapts that lifecycle for command-line use and automated test clients, while Application Testing exercises the resulting behavior across applications, requests, blueprints, configuration, templates, signals, sessions, and CLI flows. JSON Handling provides customizable serialization, response construction, and tagged values for framework helpers and sessions, while Views And Helpers supplies class-based dispatch and endpoint utilities for URLs, responses, redirects, files, flashing, and streaming. Together, these subsystems separate central lifecycle coordination from reusable interfaces and compatibility coverage while connecting through the application, context, wrapper, templating, session, and testing modules.

# Subsystem: Application Core
Application Core is the central runtime of Flask: it owns application construction, routing, request dispatch, response finalization, contexts, errors, configuration, sessions, templates, and WSGI entry. It exists separately to concentrate lifecycle orchestration in one framework boundary while allowing reusable sans-I/O scaffolding, blueprints, wrappers, and services to remain independently testable and replaceable. A request enters through `wsgi_app`, is matched and processed by `full_dispatch_request`, `preprocess_request`, `dispatch_request`, and `finalize_request`, while `Flask` delegates configuration, context, template, session, and response concerns to symbols such as `Config`, `AppContext`, `DispatchingJinjaLoader`, `SessionInterface`, and `Response`. # Subsystem: Framework Core
Framework Core is the protocol-agnostic heart of Flask: it defines the app/blueprint scaffolding, configuration loading, context-local state, request/session proxies, helper utilities, logging, template dispatching, signals, type aliases, and class-based views. It exists as a distinct unit so that the WSGI-specific `Flask` class in src/flask/app.py and the CLI/testing layers can be built on top of a stable, reusable core without coupling routing, context, or template machinery to any particular server protocol. At request time, `AppContext.push` (src/flask/ctx.py:416) and `_AppCtxGlobals` (src/flask/ctx.py:30) establish the per-request state exposed through `current_app`, `g`, `request`, and `session` proxies in src/flask/globals.py:41-62; routes and templates are wired earlier through `App.register_blueprint` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:570), `Blueprint.register` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:273), and `Scaffold.add_url_rule` (src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:376). Configuration enters via `Config.from_pyfile` (src/flask/config.py:187), `from_envvar` (src/flask/config.py:102), and `from_prefixed_env` (src/flask/config.py:126), while `helpers.url_for` (src/flask/helpers.py:200) and `templating.render_template` (src/flask/templating.py:136) tie URLs and templates back to the app. The core connects outward through related files such as src/flask/app.py, src/flask/cli.py, src/flask/json/provider.py, src/flask/sessions.py, src/flask/testing.py, and src/flask/wrappers.py, which compose these primitives into the concrete Flask runtime.

# Subsystem: Application Runtime
The Application Runtime subsystem is Flask's central execution core: the Flask class in src/flask/app.py:110 owns the WSGI application object, route registration, configuration, and request dispatch, and the supporting modules in this cluster give that object its CLI, JSON, session, testing, and request/response plumbing. It exists as a separate cluster because every other Flask subsystem (blueprints, contexts, templating, signals) must coordinate through a single hub object rather than each managing its own lifecycle; isolating the core app object keeps that coordination in one place and lets extensions inject behavior through well-defined hooks. Control flow begins when a WSGI server calls Flask.wsgi_app (src/flask/app.py:1569), which enters a request context via request_context (src/flask/app.py:1504), calls full_dispatch_request (src/flask/app.py:995) to run preprocess/dispatch/finalize, and routes errors through handle_exception (src/flask/app.py:900). The CLI side starts from the cli constant in src/flask/cli.py:1110, locates and loads an app with find_app_by_string (src/flask/cli.py:120) and locate_app (src/flask/cli.py:241), then serves it. JSON responses flow through jsonify (src/flask/json/__init__.py:138) backed by DefaultJSONProvider (src/flask/json/provider.py:124), while sessions are opened and saved by SecureCookieSessionInterface (src/flask/sessions.py:284) using the tagged serializer in src/flask/json/tag.py:219. Testing is provided by FlaskClient (src/flask/testing.py:109), which reuses the normal app dispatch path through the open method (src/flask/testing.py:204). Through related files such as src/flask/__init__.py, blueprints.py, ctx.py, globals.py, helpers.py, sansio/app.py, and templating.py, this cluster both imports and is imported by the rest of the framework, so blueprints attach routes to the app, contexts are pushed around each request, and templates are rendered inside request handling.

## Overview

`src/flask/sessions.py` is the session abstraction and adapter layer of Flask's Application layer — a central, high-betweenness bridge between the framework's request-context machinery (`app.py`, `ctx.py`, `globals.py`) and whichever storage backend holds per-request user state. It defines the session object contract (`SessionMixin`), the pluggable `SessionInterface` adapter that Flask calls at request open/save time, and the default `SecureCookieSessionInterface`, which signs a tagged-JSON-serialized snapshot of the session with itsdangerous and round-trips it through a browser cookie. The module consumes app configuration (secret key, `SESSION_COOKIE_*` settings) and the incoming request's cookie header, and produces the live session object plus the `Set-Cookie`/`Vary: Cookie` response headers that persist it. It is the contract point that makes server-side, Redis-backed, or any third-party session backend a drop-in replacement, and it is deliberately stable: 21 commits, unchanged for 90+ days, a settled and reliable part of the framework core.

## Public API

### `SessionMixin(MutableMapping[str, t.Any])`

A mixin that expands a plain dictionary into a Flask session object. It supplies the three boolean flags Flask's request machinery inspects:

- **`permanent`** (property) — reflects the `"_permanent"` key in the dict; the setter stores `bool(value)` under that key. Used with `app.permanent_session_lifetime` and `SESSION_REFRESH_EACH_REQUEST` to decide cookie expiration.
- **`new`** (class attribute, default `False`) — whether the session was newly created. The mixin cannot guarantee the backend can detect this, so it is hard-coded `False` and documented as "use with caution."
- **`modified`** (class attribute, default `True`) — whether the session changed and therefore needs to be written back.
- **`accessed`** (class attribute, default `False`) — set when the session is touched through the request context (including the global `session` proxy); when `True`, a `Vary: Cookie` header is added so caches key on the cookie. Since 3.1.3 this is tracked by the request context itself.

### `SecureCookieSession(CallbackDict[str, t.Any], SessionMixin)`

Base class for sessions stored in signed cookies. It combines Werkzeug's `CallbackDict` (which invokes an `on_update` callback on any mutation) with `SessionMixin`, and wires that callback to set `modified = True`:

```python
def __init__(self, initial=None):
    def on_update(self):
        self.modified = True
    super().__init__(initial, on_update)
```

Key caveats:

- `modified` starts as `False` here (unlike the mixin default `True`), because an empty, untouched session should not force a cookie write.
- Only direct mutations of the session dict are tracked. If the session contains a nested mutable object (e.g. `session["cart"].append(x)`), `modified` is **not** set automatically — the application must set `session.modified = True` manually.
- Because an empty session and a new session are indistinguishable after signing/verifying, `new` remains hard-coded `False`.

### `NullSession(SecureCookieSession)`

A read-only stand-in used when real session support is impossible (typically: no `secret_key` configured). Lookups work and return empty values, but every mutator is redirected to `_fail`, which raises:

```
RuntimeError: The session is unavailable because no secret key was set. Set the secret_key on the application to something unique and secret.
```

It is produced by assigning `__setitem__ = __delitem__ = clear = pop = popitem = update = setdefault = _fail`.

### `SessionInterface`

The abstract adapter every custom session backend must implement. The only required methods are `open_session` and `save_session`; everything else has useful defaults. Class-level hooks:

- **`null_session_class = NullSession`** — used by `make_null_session` and the `is_null_session` type check.
- **`pickle_based = False`** — a flag extensions can inspect to learn whether the payload is pickle-based.

Methods:

| Method | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `make_null_session(app) -> NullSession` | Instantiates `null_session_class` when the real backend cannot load. |
| `is_null_session(obj) -> bool` | `isinstance(obj, null_session_class)`; null sessions are never saved. |
| `get_cookie_name(app) -> str` | Reads `SESSION_COOKIE_NAME`. |
| `get_cookie_domain(app) -> str \| None` | Reads `SESSION_COOKIE_DOMAIN`. Since 2.3 it does **not** fall back to `SERVER_NAME`. |
| `get_cookie_path(app) -> str` | `SESSION_COOKIE_PATH` or `APPLICATION_ROOT`, else `/`. |
| `get_cookie_httponly(app) -> bool` | Reads `SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY`. |
| `get_cookie_secure(app) -> bool` | Reads `SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE`. |
| `get_cookie_samesite(app) -> str \| None` | Reads `SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE` (`"Strict"`/`"Lax"`/`None`). |
| `get_cookie_partitioned(app) -> bool` | Reads `SESSION_COOKIE_PARTITIONED` (added 3.1, for CHIPS). |
| `get_expiration_time(app, session) -> datetime \| None` | `now + app.permanent_session_lifetime` for permanent sessions, else `None` (browser-session cookie). |
| `should_set_cookie(app, session) -> bool` | `session.modified or (session.permanent and SESSION_REFRESH_EACH_REQUEST)`. |
| `open_session(app, request)` | Called at the **start** of each request, after the context is pushed, before URL matching. Must return a dict-like `SessionMixin`. Return `None` to signal non-fatal load failure — Flask then falls back to `make_null_session`. **Raises `NotImplementedError` in the base class.** |
| `save_session(app, session, response)` | Called at the **end** of each request, after response generation, before context teardown. Skipped if `is_null_session` is `True`. **Raises `NotImplementedError` in the base class.** |

### `session_json_serializer`

Module-level singleton: `TaggedJSONSerializer()` (from `flask.json.tag`). A compact JSON serializer that additionally supports Python types such as `datetime` and tuples via internal tags.

### `SecureCookieSessionInterface(SessionInterface)`

The default interface, used by every stock `Flask()` app. Stores sessions in signed cookies through itsdangerous. Class-level configuration:

- `salt = "cookie-session"`
- `digest_method = staticmethod(_lazy_sha1)`
- `key_derivation = "hmac"`
- `serializer = session_json_serializer`
- `session_class = SecureCookieSession`

**`get_signing_serializer(app) -> URLSafeTimedSerializer | None`** — returns `None` when `app.secret_key` is unset (which triggers the null-session path). Builds a `URLSafeTimedSerializer` with the current key last in the list ("itsdangerous expects current key at top" of the list it signs with) and `app.config["SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS"]` prepended for verification of older signatures.

It exists as a distinct unit so that the WSGI-specific `Flask` class in src/flask/app.py and the CLI/testing layers can be built on top of a stable, reusable core without coupling routing, context, or template machinery to any particular server protocol. At request time, `AppContext.push` (src/flask/ctx.py:416) and `_AppCtxGlobals` (src/flask/ctx.py:30) establish the per-request state exposed through `current_app`, `g`, `request`, and `session` proxies in src/flask/globals.py:41-62; routes and templates are wired earlier through `App.register_blueprint` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:570), `Blueprint.register` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:273), and `Scaffold.add_url_rule` (src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:376). The Application Runtime subsystem is Flask's central execution core: the Flask class in src/flask/app.py:110 owns the WSGI application object, route registration, configuration, and request dispatch, and the supporting modules in this cluster give that object its CLI, JSON, session, testing, and request/response plumbing. ## What this system does in one sentence

`multi-rw-flask` is a command-line-bootable web framework: `python -m flask` enters at `src/flask/__main__.py`, hands off to the CLI in `src/flask/cli.py`, and loads a Flask app from the class split across `src/flask/sansio/app.py` and `src/flask/app.py`, which then tears down each request and app context through `ensure_sync`/`async_to_sync`.

## A walk through one example

**Example: when you run `python -m flask run`**

1. **Read the map first — `README.md`.** The tour starts here because the README frames the end-to-end picture before any code: a Flask distribution that can be imported as a library or booted as a command-line tool.

2. **The process boots at `src/flask/__main__.py`.** This is the real interpreter entry point for `python -m flask`. It hands control to the CLI layer, and the next stop is `src/flask/cli.py`, where the `run` command is parsed, the target app is discovered, and the server is launched. `tests/test_apps/cliapp/app.py` is an example of an app module designed to be loaded this way — a CLI-targetable application.

3. **The app is assembled from two layers.** `src/flask/sansio/app.py` holds the I/O-independent core of the `Flask` class; `src/flask/app.py` is the I/O-bound surface that knows about WSGI and request handling. The CLI needs both: a pure core to construct, and a concrete surface to serve.

4. **Subclasses are registered, then globals resolve.** When a `Flask` subclass is created, `Flask::__init_subclass__` calls `add_ctx` to register it. From then on, any global proxy in `src/flask/globals.py` can be resolved to the live instance for the current context via `ProxyMixin::_get_current_object`. This is the hop where the static class definition becomes the concrete app handling a particular request.

5. **The request runs, then tears down.** As a request finishes, `Flask::do_teardown_request` runs its teardown callbacks; when the wider application context is popped, `Flask::do_teardown_appcontext` runs those. Both teardown flows route their callbacks through `Flask::ensure_sync`, which uses `Flask::async_to_sync` when a callback is async — bridging back into the synchronous WSGI request cycle the CLI server runs.

6. **The collaborators around these flows.** `src/flask/wrappers.py` and `src/flask/helpers.py` are the core collaborators the entry-point code reaches for — the wrappers and utilities that live beside the app and CLI layers. And `tests/test_apps/helloworld/wsgi.py` shows a bare WSGI entry point: the same app classes serving without the CLI, which is why the teardown and sync-bridging machinery lives in `src/flask/app.py` rather than in CLI-specific code.

## Why it's shaped this way

The system is shaped like a CLI front end wrapped around a library core: `__main__.py` → `cli.py` → the app classes, so the same framework can be booted from a terminal or imported by a WSGI server. Because the CLI's server drives requests synchronously, the teardown flows must normalize async callbacks through `ensure_sync`/`async_to_sync` at the points where contexts close. And because the CLI can discover and load different apps, the `__init_subclass__` → `add_ctx` → `_get_current_object` chain keeps the global proxies able to find the right app instance at runtime.

## Where to read next

- `src/flask/cli.py` — where the `python -m flask` process turns arguments into a running app and server.
- `src/flask/sansio/app.py` — the I/O-free core of `Flask` that both the CLI and WSGI entry points construct.
- `src/flask/app.py` — where `Flask::do_teardown_request`, `Flask::do_teardown_appcontext`, `Flask::ensure_sync`, and `Flask::async_to_sync` live.
- `src/flask/globals.py` — the proxy mechanism (`ProxyMixin::_get_current_object`) that connects global names to the live app/request context.

## Overview

`src/flask/cli.py` is the entry point and orchestrator of Flask's command-line interface — a central, high-PageRank Application-layer module that builds the `flask` click `Group`, resolves and loads a Flask application from import paths, factory functions, or conventional filenames, and dispatches to the built-in `run`, `shell`, and `routes` commands. It is the bridge between click's parsing model and Flask's runtime objects: it consumes app-discovery specifications (`module:name`, `module:factory(args)`, file paths, `FLASK_APP`, `-A/--app`, `-e/--env-file`) and produces a fully populated CLI whose command set merges built-ins, `flask.commands` entry-point plugins, and commands registered on the loaded app's `app.cli` group. Because `src/flask/__main__.py`, `app.py`, `blueprints.py`, and `testing.py` all import from it, and because its `cli`/`main` symbols are the process-level entry point, it sits at the center of the dependency graph (community 1, high PageRank) for everything that starts or inspects a Flask app from a terminal.

The module has three interlocking jobs:

1. **App resolution** (`locate_app`, `find_best_app`, `find_app_by_string`, `prepare_import`, `ScriptInfo.load_app`) — turning a user-supplied string or file path into a live `Flask` instance, with heuristic fallbacks for `app`, `application`, `create_app`, `make_app`, `wsgi.py`, and `app.py`.
2. **CLI construction** (`FlaskGroup`, `AppGroup`, `ScriptInfo`, `with_appcontext`) — subclassing click's group machinery so that callbacks automatically run inside an app context, eager options (`--app`, `--debug`, `--env-file`) are processed before `--help`, and app/plugin commands are merged lazily.
3. **Built-in commands** (`run_command`, `shell_command`, `routes_command`) — the default subcommands that start the Werkzeug dev server, launch an interactive shell with `make_shell_context()`, and render the URL map as a table.

## Public API

### Exceptions

- **`NoAppException(click.UsageError)`** — Raised whenever an application cannot be found, imported, or loaded. Subclassing `click.UsageError` means click renders it as a clean usage message rather than a traceback, which is why `FlaskGroup.get_command` and `list_commands` catch it to print "Error: …" in red while still allowing the CLI to continue (e.g. to list built-in commands when the app is broken).

### App discovery and resolution

- **`find_best_app(module: ModuleType) -> Flask`** — The heuristic resolver used when no explicit app name is given. It probes, in order: the `app` attribute, the `application` attribute, the *only* `Flask` instance in the module dict (raising `NoAppException` if there are multiple, with a hint to use `module:name`), then the `create_app`/`make_app` factory functions called with zero arguments. If a factory raises `TypeError`, `_called_with_wrong_args` inspects the traceback to decide whether the call itself was wrong (→ `NoAppException` suggesting `module:factory(args)`) or whether the error was raised *inside* the factory (→ re-raise, since it's the app's bug).
- **`find_app_by_string(module: ModuleType, app_name: str) -> Flask`** — Resolves an explicit spec that may be a plain name (`app`), a factory call with arguments (`create_app("dev")`), or a literal keyword call (`create_app(config="prod")`). It parses the string with `ast.parse(..., mode="eval")` and evaluates only the call node's args/kwargs via `ast.literal_eval`, so arguments must be Python literals. If the attribute is a function it is invoked with those args; the result is validated to be a `Flask` instance.
- **`prepare_import(path: str) -> str`** — Converts a filesystem path (`./hello.py`, `path/to/__init__.py`) into a dotted module name, inserting the package root into `sys.path[0]` and walking up from the file until it exits a package (no `__init__.py`). Returns the dotted name expected by `locate_app`.
- **`locate_app(module_name, app_name, raise_if_not_found=True) -> Flask | None`** — Imports the module and dispatches to `find_best_app` or `find_app_by_string`. It distinguishes an `ImportError` raised *by* the imported module (traceback depth > 1 → wraps in `NoAppException` with the full formatted traceback) from a failed import of the module itself (→ `NoAppException("Could not import ...")` or `None` when `raise_if_not_found=False`, used when scanning `wsgi.py`/`app.py`). Three `@t.overload` stubs narrow the return type for callers.
- **`_called_with_wrong_args(f)`** (private helper) — Walks the live traceback frames after a `TypeError` from a factory call; if it reaches the factory's own code frame, the factory was invoked and raised internally, so the error is real; otherwise the calling convention was wrong.

### CLI state and context

- **`ScriptInfo`** — The per-invocation state object stored as click's `obj`. Holds `app_import_path`, an optional `create_app` callback, an arbitrary `data` dict, `set_debug_flag`, and (since 3.1) `load_dotenv_defaults` — note it does *not* load dotenv itself, it only records whether defaults should be loaded later by `_env_file_callback`. `load_app()` caches the result in `_loaded_app` and resolves in this precedence order: `create_app()` callback → split `app_import_path` on `:` (via `re.split(r":(?![\\/])", ...)` so Windows drive paths survive) → scan `wsgi.py` then `app.py` in the current directory. When `set_debug_flag` is true it assigns `app.debug = get_debug_flag()` through the descriptor so dependent values repopulate.
- **`pass_script_info`** — `click.make_pass_decorator(ScriptInfo, ensure=True)`; a decorator that injects the `ScriptInfo` object as the first argument, creating one if absent.
- **`with_appcontext(f)`** — Wraps a click callback so it runs with the script's app context pushed. If `current_app` is falsy it loads the app via `ctx.ensure_object(ScriptInfo).load_app()` and uses `ctx.with_resource(app.app_context())` so the context lives exactly for the callback's duration. `ctx.invoke` preserves click's handling of callback params, and `update_wrapper` keeps the original function's metadata.
- **`version_option`** / **`get_version(ctx, param, value)`** — An eager, non-exposed `--version` flag that prints `Python X.Y.Z`, the `flask` distribution version, and the `werkzeug` version (both via `importlib.metadata.version`), then `ctx.exit()`.

### Command groups

- **`AppGroup(click.Group)`** — A click group whose `command()` decorator transparently wraps callbacks in `with_appcontext` unless the caller passes `with_appcontext=False`; its `group()` decorator defaults `cls=AppGroup` so nested subgroups inherit the behavior. *Not* to be confused with `FlaskGroup`; this is the class used for `app.cli` and `blueprint.cli`.
- **`FlaskGroup(AppGroup)`** — The top-level group for the `flask` script. Its constructor appends three eager option callbacks plus an optional `--version` option, sets `auto_envvar_prefix="FLASK"` so `FLASK_APP`, `FLASK_DEBUG`, etc. are read from the environment, registers the default `run`/`shell`/`routes` commands, and stores `create_app`/`load_dotenv`/`set_debug_flag` configuration. Key behaviors:
  - `get_command` / `list_commands` lazily load plugin commands (`importlib.metadata.entry_points(group="flask.commands")`), then merge in the loaded app's `app.cli` commands. If the app fails to load, built-in/plugin commands still work and the error is printed (colored red, no traceback for `NoAppException`, full traceback for other exceptions) instead of aborting command discovery. When an app is found, `get_command` pushes an app context via `ctx.with_resource(app.app_context())` unless one is already active — which is why `app.cli` subcommands get an app context without needing `@with_appcontext`.

# tests/test_async.py

## Overview

`tests/test_async.py` is the Test-layer entry-point suite for Flask's async support — it constructs disposable Flask applications from the `Flask`, `Blueprint`, and `View`/`MethodView` machinery and drives them through the test client to prove that async route handlers, async error handlers, async before/after-request hooks, and async class-based views all execute through Flask's async path. Because this file is never imported by other modules, it acts as a top-level orchestrator for the acceptance tests of the asgiref-backed async feature; it consumes Flask's public API and `pytest` and produces pass/fail verification that the async surface behaves identically to the synchronous one.

The suite is gated at module load time by `pytest.importorskip("asgiref")`, so the entire file is skipped on Flask installations without the optional `asgiref` dependency. Each async handler (route, error handler, hook, or view method) awaits `asyncio.sleep(0)`, forcing a real suspension on the event loop — this guarantees the test exercises genuine coroutine execution rather than a synchronous shim. Routes are registered both directly on the app (`/`, `/home`) and inside a blueprint (`/bp/`), plus two class-based views (`/view` via `View`, `/methodview` via `MethodView`), giving broad coverage of the async dispatch surface.

## Public API

| Symbol | Kind | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `AppError` | exception | Sentinel exception raised by the `/error` route; caught by the app-level async error handler. |
| `BlueprintError` | exception | Sentinel exception raised by the `/bp/error` route; caught by the blueprint-level async error handler. |
| `AsyncView` | class (`View` subclass) | Async class-based view whose `dispatch_request` awaits then returns `request.method`. |
| `AsyncMethodView` | class (`MethodView` subclass) | Async method-based view exposing `get`/`post` that await then return `"GET"`/`"POST"`. |
| `_async_app` | pytest fixture (registered as `async_app`) | App factory that builds the app under test: routes, blueprint registration, error handlers, and `add_url_rule` registration of the class-based views. |
| `test_async_route` | parametrized test | Sends `GET` and `POST` to `/`, `/home`, `/bp/`, `/view`, and `/methodview`, asserting the body contains `GET` or `POST`. |
| `test_async_error_handler` | parametrized test | Requests `/error` and `/bp/error`, asserting both return status `412`. |
| `test_async_before_after_request` | test | Builds a second, standalone app and asserts async `before_request`/`after_request` hooks fire for both app and blueprint scopes. |

Key members:

- `AsyncView.dispatch_request` — `async def dispatch_request(self)`: awaits a no-op sleep and returns `request.method`; the async analogue of Flask's `View.dispatch_request`.
- `AsyncMethodView.get` / `AsyncMethodView.post` — `async def get(self)` / `async def post(self)`: await a no-op sleep and return `"GET"` / `"POST"`, proving method-dispatching works with coroutines.

## Dependencies

- **stdlib `asyncio`** — defines the coroutines and provides `asyncio.sleep(0)` to force event-loop suspension inside handlers.
- **`pytest`** — supplies `fixture`, `mark.parametrize`, and `importorskip`; the latter conditionally skips this module when `asgiref` is missing.
- **`src/flask/__init__.py`** (cross-layer import) — provides `Flask`, `Blueprint`, and `request`; the fixture instantiates the app, registers the blueprint, and reads `request.method`.
- **`src/flask/views.py`** (cross-layer import) — provides `View` and `MethodView` base classes that the async view classes extend.
- **`tests/conftest.py`** — indirect test-layer dependency: pytest discovery and shared configuration that the fixture and test functions rely on at runtime.
- **`asgiref`** — not imported directly, but required transitively by Flask's async dispatch; the module is skipped when it is absent.

Call graph: `_async_app` instantiates `Flask` and `Blueprint`, registers `AsyncView`/`AsyncMethodView` via `add_url_rule`, and is consumed by `test_async_route` and `test_async_error_handler` as the `async_app` fixture. `test_async_before_after_request` bypasses the fixture and builds its own app to isolate hook behavior.

## Usage Notes

- Run the suite with `pytest tests/test_async.py` (or `pytest -k async`); all tests exercise the test client rather than a live server.
- If `asgiref` is not installed, the module is skipped at collection rather than failing — this keeps the test suite green on minimal Flask installs.
- The `index` route is double-decorated (`@app.route("/")` and `@app.route("/home")`), so one async function serves two paths; the parametrized path list covers both aliases.
- `test_async_route` verifies that the same async handler responds to both `GET` and `POST` — the `methods` argument on the route and on `AsyncView` permits this.
- `test_async_error_handler` relies on `async def` `errorhandler` callbacks for both the app and the blueprint, asserting the non-default status `412` propagates through the async dispatch.
- `test_async_before_after_request` uses `nonlocal` flags to confirm that async `before_request` and `after_request` hooks execute and that the `after_request` hook receives and returns the response object.
- The fixture's `return app` makes the app object directly available to tests via the `async_app` fixture name, with no teardown required since test clients are created per-test.

# Repository overview
This repository contains Flask, a Python web framework that turns WSGI requests into responses through a central application object and the Core Framework's request-dispatch and context machinery. The CLI and Testing subsystem builds on that core to discover and launch apps from the command line and to simulate requests in-process via the test client and CLI runner. JSON Support plugs into the application object as a configurable provider, handling serialization for responses and signed cookie sessions, while Views and Helpers layers optional class-based endpoints and standalone utilities on top of the core via globals like current_app and request. The Tests and Examples subsystem validates all of this behavior through the public API, using isolated fixtures and miniature applications to exercise blueprints, CLI discovery, config, templates, signals, helpers, and regression cases. Together these subsystems keep the framework's request path, developer tooling, serialization, and higher-level view patterns loosely coupled but coordinated through the application object and its associated context and response machinery.
